newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: U.S. assures Gulf leaders of security commitment.
newsitem.headline: U.S. assures Gulf leaders of security commitment.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen visited Gulf leaders and U.S. troops in Kuwait and Bahrain on Monday, telling crewmen of an American nuclear submarine that they were helping protect half the world's oil supply from Iran and Iraq.
"What keeps them at bay is you," Cohen told men from the attack ship Key West assigned to the U.S. Fifth Fleet in port at Bahrain.

Cohen, on the third leg of a trip to the volatile region that will later take him to the United Arab Emirates and Oman, also visited the U.S. guided missile destroyer Fitzgerald in Manama and sat in the control seat of its electronic-packed radar command centre.
Two glowing orange and blue screens in the darkened centre showed the position of 26 U.S. warships in the Gulf including the air force carrier Constellation off the coast of Iran.

The Secretary also visited a big U.S. armour storage site in Kuwait and met the emirs of Kuwait and Bahrain to assure them that Washigton was committed to a military presence in the region where it says Iraq and Iran are ambitious to control the oil flow.

"We are strong, we are prepared, we are reliable," he told 800 U.S. sailors and marines in a gymnasium in Manama adding that if the oil flow stopped "the economy of the world would go into a tailspin".
He was hosted at a dinner on Monday night by Sheikh Issa bin Sulman al-Khalifa, the ruler of Bahrain, after he met Kuwait's emir Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah earlier in the day.
Cohen assured Kuwait of Washington's firm commitment to its security.
"I can summarise the United States policy towards Kuwait in three words: commitment, cooperation and containment."

The Secretary said despite recent calls by some states to ease U.N. sanctions against Iraq, the United States favoured maintaining them until Baghdad complied with all 1990-91 Gulf crisis-related U.N. resolutions.
U.S. forces led an international military coalition in the 1991 Gulf War to end Iraq's seven-month occupation of Kuwait.

Cohen said U.S. policy towards Iran would not change unless Tehran showed a marked shift from its alleged support for terrorism, its keenness to buy and develop more weapons and what he said was its undermining of the Middle East peace process.
He said Iran had chemical arms under development and possibly also biological weapons while it sought to develop a nuclear capability "sometime into the future".
"We have to be concerned in terms of what the goals and designs of Iran are. Do they pose a threat to the region? We believe that they do," Cohen added.

Iran denies supporting international terrorism and says its nuclear programme is for peaceful uses. It also says its defence spending is far less than that of its neighbours although it has a much larger population and territory.

"We have seen little evidence of that (change) to date. So if there is going to be change as reflected by the most recent elections that the people of Iran wish to have change, then I think everyone in the region, as well the United States, would welcome that," Cohen added.
Last month's presidential election of Mohammad Khatami, seen as a moderate Iranian leader, raised hopes that Tehran would soften its policy toward the West. He assumes office in August.
